RagShortTexts: Between 1259 and 1261 Latin Emperor Baldwin II pawned crown relics to Venice as Nicaea.

Variants.Content: By AD 1259 the Latin Empire of Constantinople had shrunk to a perimeter behind the Theodosian Walls, and the emperor's authority reached little beyond the city itself. Baldwin II had pawned the True Cross and the Crown of Thorns to Venetian bankers to cover his debts, and palace rafters were burned for firewood because the treasury could no longer buy timber. Venice held the trade and the loans, while Michael VIII of Nicaea prepared his army across the Bosphorus. Baldwin's hollow reign lived under the constant fear that Nicaea would break through the walls and end it. The Latins' only hope lay in Western aid, and the defeat at Pelagonia had shown how little that aid could deliver when it arrived.

Behind dilapidated bastions, Baldwin II ruled over weed-choked piazzas and palaces stripped of their gold. After Pelagonia, no Western prince could be counted on to march east, and Venetian galleys could not blockade the Golden Horn forever. Every baron and clerk still serving the Latin court calculated how long Venice's loans would last, and how soon the Nicaean army would come.

Garrisons on the Golden Gate are starving, and their wages have gone unpaid for months. Across the strait, Nicaean bonfires burn bright at night. One lax watch or one unlatched sally port is all it would take for the double-headed eagle to reclaim the ramparts, and the men on the walls know it.
Greek townsfolk whisper beneath Hagia Sophia of ancient prophecies. The Latin heretics looted our sacred vessels, but true Orthodox liturgy shall soon echo beneath the great golden dome once more.
